title: 40K Weekend Update: The Lion Takes a Points Hike, Orks Bully Events
content:
Hello Dear Reader, welcome to a new column we're going to be publishing weekly here at Tabletop Battles! We've wanted to do something a little faster and more topical for a while now around 40k events, and this week we're kicking things off by talking about the major goings on of the weekend for 40k - what's happening with events and news in the space.

What about Competitive Innovations? Great question - we're still doing Comp Innovations. This article is for news hot off the presses and headlines, not deep dives into lists. If you want the quick hits on a Monday morning about the weekend's events, this is where we'll cover those. It won't always be me doing coverage

Speaking of which, we have some big news to start with this week, so let's go ahead and get things rolling:

The Lion. Credit: Jack Hunter

Games Workshop Corrects the Points on the Lion, Deathwatch Terminators

Maybe you saw Liam's unhinged rant about the Lion in our review of Codex: Space Marines and the Dark Angels Datasheets. Mabye you saw David Gaylard's YouTube video going off on the new datasheet and how the design of the Lion was absolutely insane. Either way, Games Workshop heard our collective concern and adjustments have been made. We were notified this morning that the points for both Lion El'Jonson and Deathwatch Terminators have changed. Specifically:

  • Lion El'Johnson will be 415 points on launch, not 335
  • Deathwatch Terminators will be 190 points for 5 and 380 points for 10

This is a big change, and much-needed. The Lion may still be a problem after all this - it's always hard to tell how things will play when you give a 16-wound model a 3+ invulnerable save and a 4+ feel no pain against mortals and psychic attacks - but it's at least going to actually cost you something to bring this guy. Is the Lion the new Defiler? Yeah, probably. But at least we've got a reasonable cost for him coming out of the gate.

For the Deathwatch Terminators, this is also welcome, but we suspect we're just hitting the tip of the iceberg on Deathwatch changes. Although conceptually cool as hell, the Deathwatch support Detachment really opens up a massive can of worms when you combine it with Codex: Space Marines, and the ability to combine those units with standard leaders creates some truly crazy combos.

Bad Moons Flash Gitz. Credit: Corrode

Orks Dominate the Weekend Results with 18% of TiWP Spots as Codex: Orks Hits Events

Codex: Orks properly hit the ground running this past weekend, and players were ready for it. The faction jumped from 2 event wins and 8% of TiWP (Tournaments in Winning Position Percentage) last weekend to a whopping 18% this weekend, snagging three event wins with 4 undefeated players. Next closest were Necrons at 13% and Leagues of Votann at 10%.

The most interesting part of this is that there isn't one single way to run the faction to success; Wrecaks seem to be the most common shared Detachment among the lot, though Shoota Boyz, Blitz Brigade, Dread Mob, Runt Swarm, Flyboyz, and Bully Boyz were all part of the undefeated lists over the past weekend. That speaks to both a versatile army with lots of play and a number of potential problems to solve from a balance standpoint.

Over the weekend, Orks averaged a 60.7% win rate, second most of the weekend behind Deathwatch at 61.3%. No other faction even came close to that rate - Space Wolves were next at 57.5% - though it remains to be seen if this is a fluke or not. The Deathwatch numbers are almost certainly an anomaly, given only six players played the faciton, but we recorded 46 Ork lists at GT+ events, making that a much more stable result.

A Quiet Weekend Between Challengers and LVO

It was a relatively quiet week this past weekend, with 11 GT or higher level singles events - a welcome break for Wings and Tom Lowman after the breakneck pace in recent weeks. We're in the usual lull between NOVA/Challengers Cup and the upcoming Las Vegas Open now, and the upcoming release of Codex: Space Marines figures to represent a tectonic shift for the game moving forward. Our biggest tracked event of the weekend was Münsterland Major 5 in Rheine, Germany, a 91-player, 5-round GT won by Jasper Lange running Leagues of Votann.

Credit: Warp Speed Distribution

Dumpster Fire Wins Studs and Snotlings in Ontario

Of course, this was just singles - There were also 24 Teams events we tracked this past weekend, including Studs and Snotlings in Kitchener, Ontario - a 208 player, 8-man teams event with 5 rounds run by Warp Speed Distrubition. Studs and Snotlings was won by the American team Dumpster Fire, who defeated Nasty Gamers in the final round to take home the gold. Congratulations to Ari C, Austin Warfel, Ben Greenlay, Ben Rubenstein, Dan Meloro, Jeremy Borg, Sarah Ivankovic, and TJ Lanigan for their win.

You can find the Wargames Live stream of the event here.

Games Workshop Shows of New Custodes in Their Fall Preview

GW's big fall preview showed off a few interesting things - Nobz and Legion of the Damned in Kill Team do matter for 40k players - but the big release we're going to be talking about for 40k is the Adeptus Custodes. In addition to showing off new Terminators in the WarCom preview article, their video also showed off the new statlines, revealing that even the most basic Custodian Guard will be monsters who move 8", with T7, 5 wounds, Ld 5+, and OC 3. The good(?) news is that they'll only come in units of 3 models, so we suspect we're entering a new age where Custodes armies will look more like War Dogs armies in terms of model counts, just being made up of a bunch of Space Marine captains. Their damage output also figures to be increased.

That wraps up this week's news but if you like the format or if there's something you think we should cover in future recaps, let us know - we're happy to make adjustments!

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: Dropzone Commander - Starter Box Review
content:
Hello and welcome to a review of the Dropzone introductory box, many thanks to TTC for sending a preview copy our way!

This is a rather substantial collection of sprues and the assorted accoutrement of rules and tools for playing the game once you’ve gotten enough models together to give it a spin. We’ll start into the box by diving into the models, as you’ll need to work through at least a few of those before you get to give the game itself a go and a fresh set of plastic is always exciting!

The Models

As this box is intended to be an introduction to a transport heavy game, this starter comes quite reasonably with sprues split between ground forces and the eponymous dropships that sling those forces into combat. Each side gets a pair of duplicate drop ship sprues that let you build a number of different ships classes, each with a handful of configurations, while the armies share a common ground forces sprue duplicated in sufficient number to fill out a small army of each side with some spares of a few units.

The plastic itself is about what you’d expect if you are coming from a GW game, good quality and with crisp castings that I didn’t spot any obvious miscasts on, though one bioficer model had a transparent layer of something on it that was a bit odd. The sprues are reasonably laid out, with parts that are numbered and easy enough to find, though models aren’t tightly grouped as one set of constituent parts instead a more common style of distributed across the sprue layout. Models aren’t enough pieces for this to be an overly large concern though, with each model usually only having a handful of individual pieces. The instructions are mostly straightforward, with a couple of cases of obscured steps that are slightly confusing, though the limited number of pieces and well matching part cuts mean that you can figure your way out of anything without much difficulty.

The Armies

Bioficers

A sampler of all the distinct hulls present for the Bioficers. Credit: Rockfish

Bioficers kick off strong with a ton of unique designs that admittedly can be a slightly confusing build, the ground stuff is few enough parts that it’s not too bad but you’ll definitely be flipping between the instructions and what you've got in your hands for the first few models. The aircraft might give you a bit of extra trouble as they are both large and look like an explosion in a girder factory, so you might find it tricky to give them time for the glue to set without something falling off. The end results are cool and worth the initial confusion you might encounter; every vehicle is distinct and would look great in a filled-out force.

One thing worth bringing up here is that the infantry for both sides of the box do feel a bit out of scale compared to the vehicles. This is clearly to let them have enough detail to enable painting and allow some degree of mix and match on each base but I think I’d probably have preferred lower detail smaller ones. Otherwise, the Bioficer infantry are solid, having relatively simple silhouettes on the bodies with easily read weapons, they aren’t the standout designs of the vehicles but nothing to complain about.

You will want to pick your battles as to how much effort you want to put into painting this side of the box as those distinctive designs do result in very greeble dense surfaces, this does mean that they should be good candidates for dry brushing! Though I recommend that with the caveat that you will want to phase out the sections you paint as the large panels in the designs do look very nice when clean and layered/blended.

UCM

The UCM side has the same number of distinct hulls and infantry types as the Bioficers. Credit: Rockfish

The UCM have some classic and fantastic looking staples of human forces in fiction, including dropships that I think may have won my love over the Bioficer equivelents, although admittedly the ground forces do have a few things that I found to be snaggles. Where Bioficers were able to hide the planer nature of injection molded sprues by being geometric constructs bursting to the seams with details and structure to obscure the initial state of the models, it’s much more obvious on the UCM units for better and worse because they are using more recognizable designs.

The lighter buggies and infantry both come out really great; having two similar body count infantry units at this scale is always going to be difficult to differentiate but the Legionaries and Pretorians have distinct enough garb and gear to be hard to mistake and shout out to the MA5 reference on the Legionaries being visibly different to space P90 of the Pretorians. The buggies come out pretty well too, you can only just tell their bodies are cast in one part by looking excessively closely at the wheels and with the turret you’ll never notice at all.

Things are still fine with the MBT as its hull is relatively simple in shape thanks to clearly having been inspired by modern vehicles, but there’s nothing inherently wrong with that and the turret is distinct enough you’ll get that nice bit of dimensionality to the model. The heavy tank unfortunately really suffers from the choice to make it one piece; it’s got the full combo of being a pancake with the main gun very clearly having no under cuts to split it from the hull at all. It’s disconcerting to compare it to the other units and I very much wish they’d given it a separate turret or even just split the upper hull off to give the model more depth, you can see the casting limitations far too much for being the centerpiece of the UCM ground forces.

Getting back to things I do like, the UCM drop ships are great. They use all the perfected classic design elements that were created all the classics you’ve ever loved, Aliens, Halo and every generic sci-fi movie, show or game you’ve seen the previous iterations of this concept but there’s nothing inherently wrong with that. A classic chubby little drop ship with a belly full of tank or infantry is such a fixture of the genre for a good reason! A minor complaint I’ll have on these and all the UCM vehicles is they did go a little hard on the greebling, they could have pulled back just a touch without losing any of the flavor the designs are already rich with.

The Wider Picture

Unfortunately, it’s time that an elephant is going to smash its way into the room, the flight stands the box come with are extremely poor. While the plastic rods and the rubbery piece that attaches to the ship are just as good as they were back when Dropfleet popped up, sadly here they are paired with an awful acrylic base. It's a simple laser cut square that the stick doesn’t even fit nicely into. I wasn’t impressed when I last painted a ship for my Bioficer fleet and they are no better here. I’d suggest looking to see if you can find the old bases on the secondary market or maybe using GW bases that you bore the center out a bit, as these do not glue together well and can’t be used without glue at all.

All complaints aside, I think you’ll be happy to paint either side out of this box, but I lean a little more towards the more distinctive vehicles on the Bioficer side. There’s plenty to enjoy in the plentiful plastic and most of the issues I had with the models themselves can be overlooked, plus you’ll not really have any issues with the physical act of painting as there aren’t any pockets hiding details away from you. I would have loved to get a few more things painted up in time for this article, but I'm afraid I spent rather a lot of the last month and a half sick such is life.

Supporting Infrastructure

Credit: TTCombat

They very much tried to lean into the idea of this being a starter box and for TTC that means packing in everything you need to get your first few games going, including a mat, cardboard buildings, and some tokens alongside the rules and models. How useful you find these extras will vary a bit as I found the paper mats a bit too unruly to place such light models on and the cardboard buildings are basic, they aren’t going to sit quite right or hold up to much abuse but are good enough to get started. Given you can skip the use of a mat at all or use one you have for another 6’ x 4’ game, looking at you 40k long timers, that’s not too big an issue and having enough terrain to get started is great even if you might want to upgrade before long.

The only thing missing here, at least in our review copy, is the command deck. While I think this is probably the right choice for your first handful of games, it still feels like a bit of a miss given how the box is otherwise set up to get a reasonably accurate representation of the elements in a normal game. The other thing that could have been nice to have is some simple zone templates, but the buildings meant I didn’t feel like I was missing too much here given they could be made by cutting out cardboard or paper shapes.

The Rules

Credit: TTCombat

Where mass market games like 40k have gotten increasingly word heavy and leaning ever harder on specificity to ensure the minimum of possible variants of interpretation, Dropzone is still in the design space where suggestions to be reasonable about the arcs of fire of a model and physical interactions with the board is the norm. This is honestly a good place to be for playing with your buddies, as you don’t need to engage rules lawyer brain when trying to get a fun game in with your friends but does risk some excessively argument heavy experiences with a certain sort of player.

The core rules are straightforward and common sense in general with moving and shooting that will feel familiar to anyone coming from 40k. When you get to the features more distinct to this game you will also notice how Dropzone shares a lot of DNA with Dropfleet, which is a game I’ve always enjoyed. Similar to Dropfleet, the core game loop takes place over six turns in which players alternate activating groups of units, each of which is made up of one to four squads that, hopefully given the game name, ride in a common transport. When activated, that group of units gets to move and attack, though not necessarily in that order, after their transport helpfully delivers them onto the board.

As you can expect, there’s a number of ancillary rules to help bring in more texture to the game:

  • Commanders grant your army buffs through a deck building mechanic we couldn’t explore with our review copy but look to give a variety of tools themed to each army.
  • Infantry can nesting doll their way into dropships or APC within other transports before hopping out into zones for objective play, skirmish with their counterparts in their own sub phase of an activation and can plink at armored targets when they have spare time.
  • Zones which represent various buildings or areas that have significance to the scenario and may contain scoring objectives or features that might be weapons or offer utilities to the army in control of them.
  • Ground and air units are almost different ‘levels’ with dropships only threatened by AA weapons or each other, which helps to encourage them to scoop and their charges up and across the board.

While I prefer the choices introduced by Dropfleets restrictions on movement and shooting, the Dropzone style makes for games where your forces will be in a scuffle fast. Transports are fast enough to toss their contents across a good chunk of the board which when combined with a unit fresh out of dropship being unable to attack leads to games where it’s reasonable to expect players to spend their first turn chucking out units around the board before turning on the firehose turn two. Although I found that there weren’t quite enough limitations beyond the factions in the box having weapons that are mostly short range to prevent things from turning into brawls near objectives, with the alternating nature of combat it’s easy to fall into a trap of players taking turns smashing units that emerge from cover to engage or hop on objectives.

To mitigate this a bit, the box comes with both a card of starter scenarios alongside a more substantial set in the book that have more complex scoring and table set ups that encourage more thoughtful gameplay. I don’t think I’d be too concerned with running out of distinct missions to play once you have an army and terrain collection built up a bit more, but the starter layouts are rather basic and unbalanced. Usually, these sorts of limited terrain boxes do lead to that situation, but by limiting themselves to using the included mats printed road layouts it makes for rather uneven building distribution or clear sight lines between objectives.

Tusk Tank. Credit: Rockfish

From my admittedly limited time with the game, I’d suggest avoiding scenarios with primarily end game or vehicle-based objectives, they can result in most of the game feeling a little mindless with forces beating each other up as scoring is directly linked to how much of your force remains alive. This can leave infantry occupied with rather unimportant fights inside buildings or plinking tanks, which maybe feels a little awkward given how infantry is a bit more of a rules heavy component of the game than their equivalent in Dropfleet. With some more experience I expect games can come a series of skirmishes with forces that strike before being pulled out by dropships in a back-and-forth exchange where players attempt to cut down each other’s forces while trying to hold enough in reserve for a late game push. Personally, I prefer the progressive scoring scenarios with a minimum of unit restrictive scoring, as end game scoring with only certain units able to be involved tends to result in skewed player incentives that distract from the otherwise fast pace of play.

I would suggest being a bit strategic when introducing the game to new players as the UCM side runs with conventional rules out of the book exactly as you’d expect, the Bioficiers on the other hand get an entire extra sheet of rules you need to learn to play. Lean into your inner 13-year-old and be the evil villain doing weird stuff and give your friend the UCM for the first round or two so they can focus on just learning the game. Nothing on the Bioficers is particularly complex to wrap your head around, it’s mostly mechanics to support a theme of drones puppeteered and/or spawned by support units along with being able to respawn infantry after killing enemies but it adds another layer of complexity.

While I do think you need to go into this game being aware that you’re probably not going to be seeing any serious competitive tournaments popping up near you, and you might need to be a game ambassador in your region, you will have a game that is a good excuse to spend a couple of hours pushing pretty models around a board with a friend. Speaking of, shout out to my friend Connor for taking time to help me try out the game in the busy end of summer time!

title: Neglected in the big Warhammer preview, Lord of the Rings gets grizzly new Orcs, and updated Battle Companies
content:
One major Games Workshop game was missing from the Warhammer Big Autumn Preview show last Friday: the Middle-Earth Strategy Battle Game was conspicuously absent. But as if to offer fans of The Lord of the Rings a consolation prize, this Monday the firm revealed an updated multipart plastic kit for the vicious Mordor Orcs, which will be the centerpiece of a new Battlehost army box set.

The old monopose Mordor Orcs models have been in service since 2003, so this is a most welcome refresh. The new kit will build 24 Orcs, just like the old kit, but this time they're multipart, giving you at least some cosmetic choice over how you equip them, and perhaps some gameplay flexibility.

The Warhammer Community article announcing the models states that sixteen of the models will be equipped with hand weapon and shield, with eight shield designs and eight hand weapons including swords, picks, and maces - GW doesn't mention it, but looking at the pictures it seems that a couple of these Orcs can be built with bows. The other eight can then be equipped with two-handed weapons or spears.

As well as a standalone box set, this kit will be available in a new Mordor Battlehost army set. The Orcs are accompanied by six rather Warg Riders - plastic kits that are old enough to drink - and the relatively recent model for the Witch King of Angmar, mounted and on foot.

If you're not aligned with the forces of evil, you may be pleased to hear that a new edition of the Battle Companies supplement has also been announced. This campaign mode is all about developing the story of your troops over multiple battles, collecting gold and influence for your successes while racking up injuries and fatalities.

Do you have plans to march for Mordor? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Five things D&D underdark adventures should borrow from real world caverns
content:
Down into the depths, under stone and over stone, the road wends away through cavern and cave, away from the light, into the Underdark. Adventures in the subterranean world of the Underdark are some of the most evocative in Dungeons and Dragons - and lessons from real life cave exploration can help make your party's lightless adventures feel even more real and gripping.

The ideas here all come from a trip to Blue John Cavern, a tourist attraction in the UK's Peak District which is still a site of low intensity gemstone mining. Descending the narrow steps into this awe inspiring cave system, it was impossible not to imagine how the different D&D classes might respond to such an environment.

Air and rock

Caves are created by magma forcing its way up from below, water drilling its way down from above, and other geological forces or fantastical magic - they're the children of violent ruptures in solid stone. Nothing about them is uniform. If a cavern has a flat floor, the players should ask "who leveled this out, and why?"

Caves are as likely to run vertically as horizontally, with the adjoining tunnel mouths sometimes great distances above or below the nearest flat ground. The lower portion of a cave might be a single large bowl, but the rock above it could be carved into multiple narrow channels that branch apart like a star, making spider-climbing creatures almost as mobile as ones that can fly.

Water and stone

Caves might provide shelter from the worst of the rain, but this doesn't mean they're bone dry. Water that permeates rock will flow through caves and deep caverns on its way to the aquifer, falling in waterfalls, dripping from ceilings, sweating down rockfaces, and gathering in pools. Heavy rains on the surface can suddenly flood tunnels.

Water shapes the landscape of the underdark: flowstone, stalagmites, and stalactites are all formed by the gradual deposition of calcite as it's leached from the rocks, and where these features show up, the stone is likely to be slippery underfoot.

Light and life

While caves are isolated from the surface world, they're not hermetically sealed, and surface plants and creatures will find their ways inside. If they don't find their way out, that usually spells their doom - but the presence of electric lights allows moss and algae to gradually colonize rock faces. In the magical Underdark, glowing fungi and perpetual light spells could have far more impact, creating pockets where the flora and fauna of the surface mingles with that of the underdark.

Indelible Marks

Flowstone has a surprising property - touching it with bare skin subtly discolors it, and rock that's frequently touched eventually changes from a natural white to a sickly brown-yellow. In the Underdark, discolored flowstone is a sign that a route sees frequent use - and different D&D races may leave different marks. A band of discoloration high up on a stalagmite could be a sign that ettins and ogres regularly pass through, while deep purple stains might indicate a route frequented by the Drow.

History of Use

If sentient creatures occupy a cave system they invariably rework it to suit their needs, leaving traces of their presence after they mov on. That could include steps cut into stone that follow the route into a mine, or pulley systems left in vertical shafts that once brought supplies down and treasure back up. Natural springs are likely to be dammed and directed into convenient troughs to provide clean drinking water.

In the Underdark, sentient creatures are as likely to enter a cavern from below as from above, and they're likely to make their own peculiar accommodations. Azers might unstopper magma plugs to provide light and heat; Aboleths will use magic to flood chambers that enable them to progress upwards; Beholders will widen out vertical faults to allow them to conveniently float up and down through their domain.

Has a natural wonder ever inspired you for your D&D home game? What surprising features of caves have we missed out that we should have mentioned? Let us know in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Typhoon rains off major Pokémon tournament
content:
"Inclement weather" caused the cancellation of a major Pokémon TCG tournament in Japan today, as Typhoon Dujuan hit in the midst of a national holiday. 80 mph winds batter the country, the Japanese government has issued flood and landslide warnings, and millions have been evacuated from the worst affected areas. Also, the Champions League Pokémon tournament held in Yokohama won't be going ahead today.

Only the September 21 event was cancelled, however - it still took place on September 20 and is expected to commence tomorrow, on September 22 with the main 'Masters' tournament. However, The Pokémon Company warns that "severe weather and disruptions to public transportation are expected on the day of the event", asking "all participants to check the latest weather and traffic information regularly and to prioritize safety when traveling and making decisions."

Champions League tournaments are regional competitions in Japan which, while not as prestigious as Worlds, nonetheless draw impressive crowds, with thousands of attendees. Typically there are three Champions League events each season, with the most successful players qualifying for the Pokémon Japan Championships, the country's next stepping stone on the road to Worlds.

The next Champions League kicks off in Chiba on November 22, and those with priority entry for Yokohama on September 21 will have this carried across to the Chiba contest.

Typhoon Dujuan is the 25th powerful storm to have affected Japan this year. The region is experiencing worse weather conditions than normal, due to the "super El Niño" event.

After Gen Con 2026 was hit by a tornado, it's really starting to seem like Big Wind has it out for us tabletop gamers. Stay safe out there, everyone.

title: Battle Kiwi STACK System Review
content:
As mentioned three years ago when I reviewed Battle Kiwi’s Battle Box, I am still to this day an accessory goblin-like hoarder. So when I found out Oli from Battle Kiwi was back in his design studio working on a new range of storage/gaming organisers for a range of Wargaming systems, I reached out to arrange a temporary pause in the never ending Aussie vs Kiwi debate on the origin of the Pavlova so we could instead focus on me getting my mitts on the latest evolution of his Battle Box, the Strategic Tactical Accessories Command Kit or S.T.A.C.K. for short.

We would like to thank Oli from Battlekiwi for providing us with the STACK - Core Set - 40k, the Game Mission Levels for Age of Sigmar & Kill Team along with the STACK Starter Painter set for review.

What is the Strategic Tactical Accessories Command Kit?

It’s a series of customized 3D printed trays (or layers) designed to stack together allowing you to pack and deploy various tools and accessories suitable for almost any tabletop game you care to mention.

For the Gamer

Starting with the Starter Stack is the Tools of War layer which has room for forty 16mm dice arranged in groups of five alongside the ever important tape measure and slots for all sorts of tokens you may have laying around.

Battle Kiwi S.T.A.C.K.S. - Deployment TrayThe Deployment layer has a lot of handy pieces to mark out deployment zones and useful measurement rulers in the 3”, 6” and 8” dimensions. The 3” ruler can be replaced of course with almost any flavour of 3” irregular shaped gaming pentagon measuring gauge you may have in your collection.

From this point the layers start to focus on different games where they each have a tailored layout designed to keep track whatever your game of choice needs, tracked with neat little dials and swappable tags where applicable.

Loading...

Currently Oli from Battle Kiwi has revealed trays designed for Warhammer in all her glorious forms, Infinity for the five people still playing that, Bolt Action/K47 and they have recently also revealed a tray for Necromunda. There are various trays and caddies with dividers so pretty much every game can be catered to using the STACK system especially with the options to print your own dial tags and labels.

For the Hobbyist

Battle Kiwi S.T.A.C.K.S. - Painters Range

The STACK isn’t just for the gamers, there are also trays for the weirdos that have issues with a sea of grey miniatures (I’m slowly getting better myself in this regards) as Battle Kiwi also has also provided me with their STACK Core Painter trays.

Battle Kiwi S.T.A.C.K.S. - Paint Tray

Every Core Painter set comes with a tray designed to hold assorted brushes and files as well as a removable drybrush insert that also serves as a cover for a small palette. In protecting the brushes when transporting, unless your brush fits snuggly within the slots, you will want to try and find the tiny plastic tube that vanished within seconds of removing it from the brush head… or some blu-tack.

Battle Kiwi S.T.A.C.K.S. - Contrast Tray

There are also several different trays designed to hold a wide selection of paints for all sorts of dropper bottles, enamels and whatever sized pot of citadel paint you might have. With my tray I was able to fit 24 of the Contrast pots. Each slot was nice and tight allowing you to tempt fate and hold the box upside down with the lid off.

Battle Kiwi S.T.A.C.K.S. - Transporter

For all the other tools, Oli has designed deeper storage trays that range from 5cm to 15cm that have slots to various removable buckets and doodads. There are base holders as well so whatever models you’re working on won't slide around too much and damage them. They would also be handy for transporting models for skirmish style games like Necromunda/Infinity/Blood Bowl.

How to get your hands on it.

At the time of this article, the STACK is currently available to back on Kickstarter having smashed its funding goal within hours of launching. It is set to close at the end of September with the stated goal of having the Digital print files in our hot little hands mid October through their shopfront on MyMiniFactory. Those that opt for the physical boxes will have a bit longer to wait with Oli estimating December at this stage.

Pricing at the time of writing varies on what you're after. Those that want all the digital files can pony up $79 NZD, otherwise there are small bundles for $34 NZD. Those that want someone else to do all the messing around with filament can opt to back the Physical level rewards that start out at $55 NZD all the way up to $175 NZD. You'll also need to factor in postage.

Those worried about paying through the nose for postage from Middle Earth, never fear as Oli has partnered with businesses in USA, Canada, the UK and in the land Down Under to print and post the STACKs in those countries. Sadly for the rest of the world, they’ll have to settle for the STL files.

Final Thoughts

Oli and his crew of hobbits and orks at Battle Kiwi have once again delivered yet another cool new gadget for me to play with.

Few things that we ran into in the course of this review. The dials are at first are very stiff to turn but become much smoother to rotate once rotated a few times. We also ran into some minor issues with the larger tray but since Battle Kiwi take great pride on providing excellent customer service, that was resolved very quickly with minimal fuss.

It's with mixed feelings as I ponder which game I play that gets to keep my old faithful Battle Box and I will certainly miss the faux leather lining of the dice tray but overall I will be jumping into the deep end by having backed the Kickstarter personally at the Digital STL Pro STACK - ALL IN! level. I’m keen to print up a bunch more trays for the overwhelming number of tokens, wound counters, Command Decks and so many other doohickeys that come with me as I travel with for games day.

title: Turn Order Reviews: Deified
content:
The map loads and I take a quick look at the battlefield. Three minions and a boss, who upon inspection reveals that all of the minions have to be killed before it takes any damage. That’s fine, it’s not too bad. I’ve done similar before on the first two floors. Unfortunately for me, I decide to go after my targets in the wrong order, trying to take out the one that does the most damage first and missing the fact that another one of the minions gives everyone else a second turn. This advantage turns out to be too big, and just one turn of going after the wrong enemy is enough for the fight to snowball against me, and I’m unceremoniously tossed to the game over screen a few minutes later. It takes me all of thirty seconds to decide to start a new run.

Deified is one part roguelike, one part strategy RPG. You play as Sator, a lone warrior delving into the mysterious Citadel to find a way to save his people from a mysterious calamity. The strategy parts play like a traditional SRPG, think X-Com or Final Fantasy Tactics. It’s turn-based, with Sator taking his actions and then after you end his turn, all the enemies go. You can move a certain distance each turn, and you have a few active abilities in your bar that you can use each turn. The roguelike element comes in with those active abilities, as you’ll be finding and improving them as you attempt to build a synergistic arsenal that can handle all the different challenges the Citadel throws at you.

Editor's Note: Publisher Goblinz Publishing provided a key for this review. 

Credit: Goblinz Publishing. About to rumble with my favorite boss, Sentinel 1337

Preparing to Dive

The art style is clean and almost minimalistic, without sacrificing any mood or detail. Each floor has its own distinct look that frames the protagonist and the enemies well. I really like the way the short cutscenes are composed to evoke a comic book, or maybe the kind of cutscenes you’d see in older 8 and 16-bit games. Just a lot of isolated panels popping up onto the screen and implying interaction through proximity. There’s barely a story to speak of, so the cutscenes don’t have a ton to actually SAY, but they’re a nice way to set the mood a bit before you get down to the gameplay.

Every enemy is immediately distinguishable, so once you’ve memorized all their abilities, or at least their enemy archetype, you’ll never get confused because two enemies look too similar or are a palette swap or anything like that. The only real visual issues I had are that sometimes traps will fire from an area of the screen that makes them hard to see. You’ll always know where they generally are, but sometimes you just don’t see that arrow trap sticking out of a wall.

Credit: Goblinz Publishing. Chatting with Eris, before we fight her

Tackling the Citadel

When you start a run in Deified, you’re presented with a hex map that has a bunch of different types of encounters on it. The vast majority of them are a combination of shop and enemy encounter. You’ll rummage through the different kinds of relics you can add on your bar, with each action you take, like rerolling your choices or spending gold on a relic, making more noise. This noise mechanic adds a good amount of tension to runs. If you keep the noise level low, you can bypass the standard combat encounter that would be there, at the cost of not getting very many looks at the shop and any resources like gold and experience you would’ve gained from defeating your foes. On the other hand, refresh too much or buy too many things and you’ll put the enemy in an alerted state, upping the difficulty of the upcoming fight.

The moment-to-moment SRPG gameplay is fantastic. The abilities you get are extremely varied, and trying to make something work out of a weird combination of relics you’ve never tried before is really fun, at least in the early encounters when things haven’t ramped up too much. The different relics aren’t just slight cosmetic or damage type differences, they dramatically change the best way to tackle a map. My favorite example is the Empusa relics. They’re more powerful than the other relics, with the drawback that they cost health to use, a big drawback in a game where healing is at a premium. Get more than one, though, and all of a sudden all the blood puddles that you’ve been creating when you hit someone take on a whole new meaning as walking over a tile one is on can heal you. This changes your turns into what’s almost an exercise in accounting: can you generate enough blood and movement to make using these relics break even, or even turn that drawback into a benefit?

Credit: Goblinz Publishing.  The victory screen, showing various currencies.

In between runs you have two separate meta-progression mechanics, one to upgrade the map itself and the encounter types on it, and one to upgrade Sator himself. These share resources, so they’re going to take a whole lot of time and runs to complete. I haven’t gotten anywhere close to maxing out anything and I’ve put in a good fair number of runs. These upgrades are key to tempering the really mean difficulty of Deified. The game is just incredibly difficult until you start unlocking things like giving Sator health whenever an enemy dies or until you’ve added a few more healing fountain encounters to each floor.

Where things get a little unsatisfying is the special boss mechanics that would work fine in your typical slay the spire-like but are really annoying in an SRPG context. There are bosses that want you to balance attacking multiple enemies, or to do things in a specific order that become very difficult/impossible once you take the action and movement limitations into account. The Vault boss is a good early example.

The Vault has a ton of armor, more than can be reasonably burned through by any number of attacks, and the total refreshes every turn. To strip the armor from him, you have to kill one of the minion enemies that spawn with him, and occasionally respawn. Once you kill one, you have the rest of that turn to damage him. If everyone is all standing in a huddle beating on each other? That’s not so bad, just spend at least one action on a minion and then go to town on the boss. However, if you can’t stack them up, you can’t efficiently move between enemies and the fight just drags on because the minions are real, legitimate enemies from earlier in the floor. They’re not bespoke  one-shottable enemies that are just there to enable the gimmick. They take multiple turns to kill, so if you blow one chance it gets really annoying.

Or, you take the upgrade that shows you who the floor boss is going to be and you don’t fight the Vault until you’ve got a move that hits hard and ignores armor altogether. Sorry about those first runs, kid.

Credit: Goblinz Publishing. Starting to take on a final boss

Too Much of a Good Thing

While each fight in Deified is individually engaging, by the time you get to the third floor the runs are starting to take a very long time, more than I want to spend in one sitting. Even when I skip most of the fights on the third floor and head straight for the boss, runs easily clear an hour and some get towards an hour and a half. That’s before you get to the final boss, where, depending on which final floor you chose, it might have a gimmick that makes the fight take forever.

It’s not a passive hour and a half, either. Each fight has the potential to go sideways extremely quickly, leaving you in a hole of low health that can take the entire run to recover from if you get unlucky or don’t have a healing ability in your tool kit. There are no fights you can just autopilot through, which makes for a fantastic challenge but eventually wears you down.

The obvious solution is to just take a break, but then you get into the other issue: there’s just too much stuff for me to remember to leave and come back. I’ve got 5-6 abilities, each of which has some kind of drawback and advantage to it thanks to how the slot modifiers work. Each floor has totally different enemies with their own gimmicks that need their own strategies. I have synergies that range from nice to have to totally run defining. It’s a lot, and as soon as I close the game it all vanishes, leaving me to pick it all up again only without the muscle memory I’ve built up. There are no great choices there.

Credit: Goblinz Publishing. A few rounds after encountering that final boss.

One More Run

Deified is a deep, engaging strategy game that has a tendency to overstay its welcome. I can heartily recommend it to anyone who wants to play an SRPG that has you reacting on the fly from fight-to-fight, where you’re never really sure what’s coming next. Just have a better memory than I do, or take some notes when you need to call it a day in the middle of the run.

title: How to play Pokémon cards for beginners
content:
Looking for a beginner-friendly guide that'll teach you how to play Pokémon cards? The Pokémon TCG rules are super approachable, and there are plenty of pre-made decks that can make your first battles even easier. We can walk you through the basic rules, from finding a deck to declaring victory.

What is the Pokémon card game?

Pokémon cards aren't just good for stuffing in binders, they also allow you to play the Pokémon TCG. In this strategy game, players take it in turns to play cards, and attack each others Pokémon, claiming prize cards for each Pocket Monster you KO. The first to six prize cards is the winner.

What is a Pokémon deck?

Your deck is the set of Pokémon cards you use to defeat your opponent and win the game.

A Pokémon deck includes 60 cards. Within, you'll have a mix of Pokémon cards, the pocket monsters you know and love; Trainer cards representing useful items or human characters helping you out; and Energy cards, which you'll attach to your Pokémon to power their attacks.

There's only one other rule to bear in mind when creating your deck, which is that you can't have more than four copies of any one card. If you're totally new to the Pokémon TCG, we recommend you read our full breakdown of what all these cards do and how to read them, below. But if you'd rather get straight into a battle and learn as you go, skip straight past to 'How to set up a game'!

Pokémon card types

Just like in the Pokémon videogames, each 'mon has an elemental 'type' that affects its strengths and weaknesses (Decidueye above is Grass-type, shown by little leaf symbol). However, the trading card game has far fewer types than the videogame.

The 11 Pokémon card types are:

  • Grass type
  • Fire type
  • Fighting type
  • Dragon type
  • Fairy type
  • Darkness type
  • Colorless type
  • Psychic type
  • Lightning type
  • Water type

If you want to learn more about those, we have a whole guide to Pokémon card types you should read after this one. To begin with, though, we just need to learn about the four overall types of Pokémon cards in the game:

  • Basic Pokémon
  • Evolution Pokémon
  • Trainer cards
  • Energy cards

Basic Pokémon

During the game, you'll start by playing Basic Pokémon, using Energy cards to power them up, and then using their attacks to try and knock out your opponent's Pokémon.

Evolution Pokémon

You'll then evolve them into Evolution Pokémon to make them stronger, using their more powerful attacks, defeating more enemy Pokémon, and eventually winning the game.

Trainer cards

Trainer cards are used to support these efforts by giving you extra benefits or disadvantaging your opponent in some way. These cards represent the items, supporters, and stadiums a Trainer can use in battle.

They allow you to heal Pokémon, draw more cards. and do special actions (such as switch your active Pokémon with a benched Pokémon). Some are simple, one-time boosts, while others tweak the game in complex and subtle ways that will work really well for some strategies, but harm others.

Energy cards

Energy cards are attached to Pokémon to power up their attacks (or retreat if they're starting to look hurt).

There are lots more sub-categories of cards you'll encounter on your Pokémon TCG journey, from Supporter Trainers to special ex, V, VMAX, and VSTAR Pokémon cards - but you don't need to worry about that stuff yet.

The ratio of card types in a Pokémon deck varies greatly depending on what cards you want to play with. As a baseline, we'd recommend including 10 to 20 Pokémon, 8 to 15 Energy cards, and as many Trainers as you can with the cards left over.

How to set up a Pokémon card game

To set up a Pokémon card game, players shuffle their 60-card deck and draw a hand of seven cards. Each player then places a Basic Pokémon (identified in the top left-hand corner of the card), face down. This is their active Pokémon, which can battle and take damage.

If a player does not have a Basic-level Pokémon available, they must reveal their hand to their opponent, shuffle their cards back into their deck, and draw seven new cards. This is called a 'mulligan'. Each time a mulligan is performed, the opposite player may elect to draw an extra card.

Players can then place up to five Basic-level Pokémon, face down, onto their bench area. Next, players draw another six cards from the top of their deck and place them face down to the side of the play area, without looking at them. These are your Prize Cards.

Finally, players flip a coin to determine who will go first, and then flip their active and benched Pokémon face up. It's finally time to battle! The first player cannot attack on their first turn, and neither player can evolve a Pokémon on their first turn.

How to play Pokémon cards

There are three turn phases in the Pokémon TCG:

  1. Phase 1 - draw a card.
  2. Phase 2 - Add Basic Pokémon to your Bench; attach one Energy to a Pokémon; play Trainers; Retreat your active Pokémon; use Pokémon abilities.
  3. Phase 3 - Attack with your active Pokémon.

Here's a full breakdown of how each of those parts work in games:

Phase one

Draw a card from the top of your deck.

Phase two

Perform any of the following, in any order:

  • Place a Basic Pokémon card from your hand on your Bench face-up. Your bench can hold a maximum of five Pokémon.
  • Evolve a Pokémon.
  • Attach up to one Energy card from your hand to any one Pokémon.
  • Play Trainer cards from your hand (you may only play one Supporter card and one Stadium card per turn).
  • Retreat your active Pokémon by discarding energy from it equal to its Retreat Cost, and replace it with a benched Pokémon.
  • Use any number of your Pokémon's Abilities (listed in red on the card).

Phase three

Attack, using one of your active Pokémon's attacks. To use a Pokémon's attack, you need to have enough Energy attached to meet the energy cost. You don't have to discard this Energy to make the attack, unless it says so.

Once your active Pokémon has made its attack, your turn ends. It's now the other player's go!

How to attack in the Pokémon TCG

Each turn, you may make up to one attack using your active Pokémon. After the attack is fully resolved, your turn ends, and it's now your opponent's turn (unless you just won the game, of course!)

Each Pokémon has one or more attacks, which are listed underneath its picture. These have four pieces of information:

  • The attack name.
  • The Energy required to use the attack.
  • The amount of damage the attack deals.
  • The effects of the attack, if any.

To use an attack, the Pokémon must have Energy attached to it equal to or greater than the attack's Energy requirement. Normal (white) Energy requirements can be met with any type of Energy - otherwise you need Energy of the correct type.

Almost all attacks deal damage to your opponent's active Pokémon. For every 10 points of damage, place one damage marker on the opponent's Pokémon as a reminder. If a Pokémon ever has as much or more damage than its total HP, it's knocked out!

Many attacks have additional effects. These are written under the name of the attack. They could do almost anything: they might deal damage to Pokémon on the enemy bench, deal extra damage if you win a coin flip, force you to discard Energy from the Pokémon that made the attack… anything!

Pokémon resistance and weakness

The bottom of a Pokémon card list its elemental weakness and its elemental resistance. These will indicate an energy type, and a sum. For example, a Pokémon might have Darkness weakness x2, and Fire Resistance -30.

These modifiers apply to the damage the Pokémon receives from attacks made by a Pokémon with the relevant elemental type. You can find A Pokémon's elemental type in the top right corner of its card.

The Talonflame in the video above has Lightning weakness x2: it takes double damage from attacks made by Lightning type Pokémon. It has Fighting resistance -30: it takes 30 less damage from attacks made by Fighting type Pokémon.

Remember: it's the type of the attacking Pokémon that matters for resistance and weakness. It doesn't matter what type of energy was used to power up the attack.

How to knock out Pokémon in the TCG

When a Pokémon has received at least as much damage as its total HP, it is knocked out. The Pokémon card, plus any Energy cards or item cards attached to it, and any Pokémon cards that it evolved from and which are underneath it, are sent to the Discard pile.

It doesn't matter where this damage comes from. Pokémon usually take damage from being attacked by your opponent's Pokémon, but they might also suffer damage from the Poisoned status, or even from their own attack! These can all knock out a Pokémon.

When a Pokémon in the active spot is knocked out, its controller moves a Pokémon from their bench into the active spot to replace it - if they can!

How to evolve Pokémon

To evolve a Pokémon in the Pokémon TCG, you simply place the card showing the evolved form of that Pokémon on top of it. You can do this whether the Pokémon you want to evolve is in the active zone or on your bench.

You can evolve any number of Pokémon during your turn, before you attack. There are limits:

  • You can only evolve each Pokémon once per turn (so no going from a basic to a stage 3 in one turn).
  • You can't evolve a Pokémon the same turn it is played to your bench.
  • You can't evolve a Pokémon on your first turn.

Evolving a Pokémon doesn't heal it from any damage, but it does remove any debilitating status conditions causing it problems, which can come in handy. Pokémon Tools or Energy cards attached to your Pokémon will stay attached when you evolve.

You'll usually want to evolve Pokémon in every single game you play. That's because evolved Pokémon cards are typically much stronger, with more HP and more powerful, damaging moves.

How to use Energy cards

Pokémon energy cards are vital to powering up your Pokémon's attacks. Each turn, you may attach one energy card to one of your Pokémon.

Basic energy cards are the most common. Unlike other cards, you may have any number of Basic energy cards in your deck. They represent one of the different elements used in the game:

  • Fire
  • Water
  • Grass
  • Lightning
  • Fighting
  • Psychic
  • Metal
  • Darkness
  • Fairy

Each basic energy card provides exactly one energy of the relevant element.

Additionally, there are special energy cards. These have additional, unusual effects. They are limited to a maximum of four copies per deck, like other cards.

Can I attach more than one energy card to a Pokémon during a turn?

Normally, you are restricted to attaching one energy card to a Pokémon each turn. However, some Pokémon attacks, or abilities, and some trainer cards, allow you or instruct you to attach additional energy cards to one or more of your Pokémon.

In that case, the additional energy don't count against the one per turn limit. You can use that ability, and still attach one energy card to a Pokémon.

How to use Pokémon TCG Abilities

Pokémon TCG abilities are special, activated effects that some Pokémon have. These are indicated on the card with a title written in red. Usually, these are listed under the card art, and above any attacks.

Every ability is unique. It tells you what it is, and when you can use it. You can only use an ability once per turn, but the right ability at the right time can change the course of a whole battle!

How to win Pokémon cards

There are three ways to win a game in the Pokémon TCG. The first involves the Prize cards you placed to one side during setup.

  • Each time you knock out an opposing player's Pokémon, you draw one of your six Prize cards. Some Pokémon are so powerful - like Pokémon ex, or Pokémon VSTAR, that they grant additional Prize Cards when they're knocked out. The first player to take all of their Prize cards wins.
  • You win if your opponent has no active or benched Pokémon left in play.
  • You win if your opponent has no cards in their deck when they go to draw at the beginning of their turn.

How to play Pokémon cards online

Currently, there are two digital versions of Pokémon worth playing:

Pokémon TCG Live

Pokémon TCG Live is a digital recreation of the paper card game, with cards that work exactly the same as their cardboard counterparts. Everything you learned above still applies.

Sadly, your physical Pokémon card collection can't be transferred directly into the digital game, card by card; they're two separate things. However, all kinds of physical Pokémon TCG products, including booster packs, pre-built decks, and more, all come with a Pokémon TCG Live code card inside.

Use the Pokémon TCG Live app to scan the QR code on these cards, and you'll unlock a parallel, digital version of the same product to open and add to your personal, online collection - be it a booster pack of random new cards, or an entire deck of listed cards.

If you've got some older physical Pokémon card packs that have Pokémon TCG Online codes instead of Pokémon TCG Live ones, don't worry - they'll still redeem fine on the new platform.

Pokémon TCG Pocket

Pokémon TCG Pocket is a streamlined version of the Pokémon TCG created specifically for mobile phones. A lot of the focus of the game is on opening virtual card packs, and the deck-building and battles are far simpler than the original. The upside of this is that it's a great way for newbies to ease themselves into the rules - however, you should be prepared for a slight increase in complexity if you want to try the full game afterward. 

Choosing your first Pokémon deck

You can build a Pokémon deck yourself (and the linked guide can help you do so), but we recommend using a pre-built deck for your very first game. The top products to pick up are either a Battle Deck or the Battle Academy starter set.

Battle Decks

Battle Decks include not only a well-composed deck ready for you to play, but also a folded paper playmat to play on, some helpful game tokens, a deck box to store your cards, and a nifty plastic coin (some Pokémon cards require you to flip a coin, and it's always better when you use a shiny Pokémon TCG coin instead of a regular penny).

They also come in handy double packs like the Lycanroc vs. Corviknight bundle below - giving you two full decks, ready to play!

These decks will not win you a tournament, and they will struggle against another player who has constructed their own deck. However, they are good for casual play, especially against other people who also bring a Battle Deck to the table. If you have a group of friends, buy a few different decks, shuffle up and start playing.

Battle Academy starter set

The Battle Academy starter set makes things even simpler: it's a single $20 box that contains three very basic 60-card starter decks, all the supporting bits and bobs from the battle decks, and a proper folding cardstock playing board with space for both players' cards.

The included decks won't take you very far once you've learned the ropes - but it's an excellent, cheap way to get started with no muss and no fuss.

Looking for more? Here's all you need to know about legendary Pokémon. Plus, our sister site Pocket Tactics are true Pokénuts, with a complete guide to all the Pokémon in the Pokédex.

title: Hobby Build Academy: Storing Extra Pieces, or My Pal Stanley
content:
Welcome back to another week of Hobby Build Academy; this week we're taking a bit of time to talk about something that becomes exceptionally more important the more you hobby, which is primarily the question: "What do you do with the extra pieces you have left over"? This is a pretty common question that can come up for Gunpla, LEGO, and almost any type of model building (as many of you 40k players can attest), but if you're a very new or just starting hobbyist, knowing the best way to store said pieces can always be a bit of a conundrum. So this week, your Professor, Marcy, and her assistant, Elly, will talk about a few good, easy, and namely inexpensive ways to tackle storage considerations for your hobbying regardless of your level, from beginner to old hand.

Beginner Storage: Don't Toss That Box!

Marcy: I know that some may consider tossing out the box to your first Gunpla model as standard, while others may say keeping empty boxes is hoarder behavior, but I think there's actually something very helpful in the middle: using the box as storage for your first few model kits! Your first model itself is likely to have some extra pieces, such as alternative hands, weapons, or even very minor cosmetic options; for example, the HG GQuuuuuuX I built came with a few armament options and the ability to make the backpack into a separate standing piece.

Elly: I do think it's fair to not want to keep an empty box around if you have no use for it; I tend to do a lot of junk journaling, so I'll often cut out a key art or photograph from a box and use that when I journal, while getting rid of the rest, but I do think that from our first few models, I've made a lot of use out of the HG Zaku box to store things, which was further helped by some light organization tips.

You wouldn't believe how much stuff this box fits.

Marcy: Organizing is honestly your area of expertise, so I'm going to let you take the stage here.

Elly: I think just tossing everything into an empty box is not really as sound advice as it could be; obviously it is better than nothing, but what I further suggest is using small ziplock bags (assuming you have them) and putting your excess parts in there. Then, you can also store your hobby tools, as well as the instruction manual if you want; that's about the only thing I've really cared to keep from most of the kits I've done so far. So far, we've actually managed to store almost every model kit we've done's extras in this single HG box, along with two pairs of nippers, a hobby knife, silicone pushers, and and more. The biggest thing for organizing is actually organizing; just tossing everything into a box is not going to work.

Marcy: For LEGOs, I think this works roughly the same; we built a set of Christmas Trees last Christmas, and I've been using that box with the aid of some baggies to help separate the extra pieces from that. Honestly, I will say that we have a lot more left over LEGO pieces than we do Gunpla pieces, so depending on how many LEGO sets you're building, this solution--reusing the box and some bags--may only work for a bit of time, but so far we haven't had to fully upgrade. Yet. But even just this box was enough to organize the extras from these Christmas Trees, a Catcus set, a bouquet, the Japanese Plum Blossom set, as well as their instruction manuals, so I think it really isn't hard to still get a lot of value out of a sturdy box.

Intermediate: The Stanley Parable

Elly: Okay so first we should probably say we are not sponsored nor are we specifically saying you should buy a Stanley product, right?

Marcy: Correct! I'm simply just unable to resist a good pun, but I also think that many people will likely immediately clue in on what we're talking about with the name drop; essentially, we're talking about tool-box organizers, which Stanley, the brand, is very famous for.

Elly: Yeah, these tool-box organizers are pretty universal, we've seen versions of them at IKEA, hardware stores, even "department" stores like Target; I think I even saw variety at Michaels. Realistically, the thing you want here is a box with a snapping lid and usually transparent top that allows you to see what is inside of it once you've organized things, and that comes with compartments of various rectangular or square sizes that let you place things inside of securely.

A tacklebox organizer like this from PLANO is also a great option; I really like the adjustable pieces which can help with awkward sized LEGOs or Gunpla parts, although width can be an issue too.

Marcy: The reason I don't actually suggest these for a new hobbyist is that they are going to add cost to your hobby; even a cheap one is still going to run probably around 15~ USD, and while 15 USD is maybe not a lot of money, it is also not nothing; if you have just bought your very first Gunpla or a few models, 15 dollars is roughly half the cost of most HG models. There is also just frankly the honest statement that you don't need this for a long time unless you are building multiple models a week and are going to be swimming in parts.

Elly: I think that's the biggest point to make here at the intermediate level, which is also very important for beginners or cost conscious hobbyists: it can be REALLY easy to go all out and spend, spend, spend on your hobby because the initial dopamine rush can really urge you to buy every little thing you could possibly want or need; the reality is that you're putting out a lot of money for things that are going to see very little use or utility for a long time; the only reason we even needed to get Micro Sol and Micro Set right away was because I decided to start with a waterglide model; the same goes for storage. If you have a box like this that you can repurpose, then you should absolutely consider it, but don't buy more clutter to "de-clutter" when you are going to place a single energy sword or posable hand into it and nothing else for months.

Marcy: For LEGO, I think you could argue this might become more useful faster, but that actually really only matters if you have a lot of left-over pieces, and plan to do customized builds or utilize those pieces; I do foresee us using a tackle-box or tool-box style system though once we get through a few more bigger sets, which are likely to have considerable left-overs and make sorting them much more likely to be valuable.

Experienced: Systems and Shelving

Elly: So again, probably not something that should be done unless you've got a pretty large collection, right? We're almost about to suggest buying furniture.

Marcy: Yes, this is probably something most people are going to want to consider working towards, or if they are currently staring at a fairly large collection, a few solutions to organizing said collection; note that this isn't really advice on displaying your models, just storing the extra pieces! Displaying is a whole other puzzle to tangle with, one that is even more space restricted than storage is.

Elly: Right! So with that out of the way, I think... well, you might not be that surprised, reader, but we're still going to suggest tool-boxes and tackle-boxes! At least, for the first few. Again, not to name drop specifically, but Stanley makes a band of boxes called "Fatmax" that have particularly deep containers, while also having them in a few different sizes. Just from having built and taking a look at some of our bigger kits, both Gunpla and LEGO, awkward sized extra pieces are pretty common, which make storing them a bit more difficult. The nice thing is that these tool-boxes are generally stackable.

Stanley keeps making these and naming them all sorts of things every few years; realistically, you just want to look for something that visually looks like this and is around 30 dollars.

Marcy: I actually own a set of similar boxes that I use for my miniatures, and they not only stack, they interlock with one another. It makes it really easy to put the entire army away while also allowing things to be organized in a way that makes sense; I think my boxes were primarily organized by painted, built and unpainted, and unbuilt/extras.

Elly: Beyond that, our final suggestion might sound a little unorthodox, but instead of building a specific furniture piece, I mostly want to advocate for utilizing a bookcase or shelving unit alongside labeled boxes, similar to tupperwares or other closed lid plastic tubs. I really don't want to make it sound like I'm saying "Hey! Go buy a Billy bookcase and a bunch of quart tubs!" but that is kind of what I'm saying. At least, if you have a bookcase/shelving unit available to you, making use of it with tubs and storage containers can be good for exceptionally large collections. They help keep your pieces safe, they keep them away from dust or other environmental things like sunlight, and they can reduce the possibility of loss or breaking by being in a place you are unlikely to have them moved.

Marcy: Of course, you have one other aspect to offer here, I assume.

Elly: Correct: labels. You absolutely need to label these boxes! When I see collections of things without labels, it drives me up a wall; the thing is that while putting things in tubs or containers is really helpful and honestly a very good way to keep things organized, it can be very easy to forget what is even in the box without some sort of label. If you want to go for the very least required, using some masking tape or store-bought single labels with things like "Weapons", "Hands", etc. could be great. But I'd even advocate going a bit beyond that and making comprehensive lists that you can tape to the top of the box, or if space allows, the side of it. That way, you know EXACTLY what is in the box, not just a general idea, and when you get more things that fit that category, you can easily put them in those boxes without having to redo a lot of your organization.

Wrap-Up

Before we go, I wanted to note something that is actually pretty useful for organization but gets overlooked a lot: Holiday storage. Very likely, Halloween merchandise is now on your store shelves, and Christmas stuff will probably start appearing in the next week or so; throughout the Holiday season, you'll start seeing a lot of holiday storage that can be VERY helpful for all sorts of hobby storage. The irony is these are often sold cheaply and even at great discount as the holidays end, but unless you absolutely hate the idea of storing your stuff in Green or Red boxes, they can be an absolute steal. Our Beyblade stadium is housed in a Christmas Wreath bag, and it's the best thing to ever fit it; don't overlook holiday storage! Next week we'll be back with a set of model kit reviews; we've been pretty busy in the background! Until then, stay building and we'd love to see what you're working on either in the comments or on Discord!

title: MTG Reality Fracture infinite combo creates a deadly dragon disaster with only two cards
content:
Reality Fracture has brought a treasure horde of exciting new cards to Magic: The Gathering and fans are hard at work figuring out all sorts of exciting new ways to break them. One of these spectacular combos will fill the skies with an infinite number of dragons, but you'll be forced to call it a tie unless you have a way to break the chain.

This infinite involves the new card Draconic Visitor, which has a replacement effect that makes artifact tokens come in as 5/5 dragons. Ganax, Astral Hunter makes a treasure token when it or another dragon enters the battlefield. If you play both of these cards, in either order, you set off an endless combo, as each new dragon makes a treasure that ends up coming out as yet another dragon.

This is one endless dragon army you might wish you could put back in the bottle, however, because neither of these abilities are optional. The rules of Magic: The Gathering state that if a loop consists of an endless chain of mandatory actions which neither player can or will break, the game will end in a draw. Which is a sad result when you have an uncountable number of big flying beaters waiting in the wings.

If you have a kill spell you can put down one of your own combo pieces to stop the madness. Otherwise, your best bet is the card Impact Tremors. This will damage everybody else when your dragons enter play, ultimately defeating everyone at the table.

This is not the only dragon-related combo worth mentioning in the set. Niv-Mizzet might be a ghost in Jace's new multiverse but he's still up to his old tricks: drawing an impossible number of cards.

In this case rather than the enchantment Curiosity, he has an unlikely teammate: Sheoldred. That's because the new Niv, Niv-Mizzet Ghost Counsel lets you pay life whenever you gain life to draw cards. Sheoldred the Apocalypse has you gaining two life whenever you draw, so with both out on the field, you can easily draw as many cards as you like.

title: Contemptor Kevin's Combat Patrol Issue 67 Review
content:
The Genestealer Cults continue to pour into the Combat Patrol battlefield from the hiding spots in the corners and undergrowth of Hive Worlds, with the first half of the second squad of Neophyte Hybrids.  In addition to the models and instructions, we also get a short story, campaign, and 10th edition Index rules for the Combat Patrol.  Will they successfully rise up and overthrow the rotten Imperium and pave the way for the arrival of the Star Children?  Let's find out!

As always, thank you to Tabletop Battles and Hachette for the opportunity to review these models, magazines, and materials.

Hobby Materials

This issue comes with the first half of a second unit of Neophyte Hybrids. It's the same sprues as Issue 64. Furthermore, the assembly instructions for the Hybrids are exactly the same as the instructions in Issue 64: Unlike the 2021 Ork Boyz (but like the starter set Tyranid Hormagants), it's the same weapons loadout and special weapons, the only real difference is probably going to be which head goes on which body. I'm a little surprised that this Combat Patrol has two of the same unit, but it is what it is.

Neophyte Hybrids. Credit: Rockfish

Narrative Materials

This issue has one article. It's a four page story that, unusually for a 40K short story in Combat Patrol does not have a completely depressing ending. The viewpoint character of the short story "Insurrection" is Guardsman Kyser during a confusing and chaotic firefight. Guardsman Kyser volunteers to go man a heavy bolter against the enemy, and his sergeant sends a pair of Guardsmen with him for cover. They were two of the Sergeant's longtime troops, and "she knew they could be relied upon." So into the fog of war they charged across the battlefield to the Heavy Bolter. The get to the heavy bolter and start pulping the mysterious enemy combatants when they receive orders to halt fire. They don't know why when Goliath Rockgrinders began an attack run, and additional insurrectionists follow behind them. Unfortunately, heavy bolters aren't great against Rockgrinders! Kyser shoots at the windows of the Rockgrinder, and eventually caused the trucks to spiral out of control.

Credit: BuffaloChicken

Additional insurrectionists pop out of the Rockgrinders, wielding heavier and better weapons and advancing through the smoke. Then Guardsman Kyser runs into another problem: Guardsman Raphe gets sniped and Guardsman Mattias attacks Guardsman Kyser! Mattias pulls a knife on Kyser, and has become sickly pale, black nails, and with visible forehead ridges. Hybrid Mattias stabs Kyser, screaming about how "The chains of tyranny are broken. All hail the coming of the Star Children!" The wounded Guardsman Kyser can see the mad zealotry behind Mattias' eyes.

Then Mattias' head explodes because Sergeant Kolson arrives, pulling her trooper to his feet. She gives him a gun, and they regroup with a few of their troopers. They can now see the insurrectionists, many Cadian uniforms amongst the labourers assaulting the Imperial lines. Sergeant Kolson requests fire support on their position: The situation does not appear to be survivable, and so the Guard need to drop artillery on their position. Sergeant Kolson has her troops regroup to flee the sector, and realize they are alone and isolated.

But hey, for once in a Combat Patrol short story, they aren't dead, dying, or effectively doomed.

Gaming Materials

The most useful gaming material is on the back cover of the issue: multiple Cult Ambush tokens. Given the token-heavy nature of modern 40K nowadays, getting free tokens with faction theming is pretty nice. We get a blurb to give this faction a different set of potential backgrounds for the second Hybrid units. We also get two new Campaign entries: Genestealer Cults vs. Space Marines, which features Genestealer colonials fighting against a Space Marine force seeking ancient archaeotech. The second mission is a bit more thematically fun: Genestealer Cults vs. Tyranids. The Day of Ascension has come! The Star Children have arrived! The Cults' plans have come to fruition and the revolution has succeeded!

Unfortunately, the Hive Fleet wants to eat them. And the Cultists do not necessarily want to be eaten. Perhaps it is a test of faith.

The rest of the gaming material is about the Genestealer Cults' faction abilities, stratagems, secondary objectives, and enhancements. Cult Ambush is an army ability that will allow defeated units to return to the battlefield, and the units of the Combat Patrol can absolutely make full use of this ability. The enhancements available to this Combat Patrol were +1 save to the Magus against ranged attacks, or give her staff [Anti-Infantry 5+] and [Devastating Wounds].

The Final Verdict

For the most part, this issue is pretty similar to issue #64, down to having a focus on campaign mode and a short story. The difference is that this is 1) the second time around we are getting this particular set of models but 2) the short story is complete and self-contained. So if I had to choose between getting *one* of either Issue #64 or #67, issue #67 is probably the better choice.

Until next time Combat Patrolers!
